name: Felix Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix, 43, and I drive a haul truck at the large mine. I've got a vocational certificate and enough time on the route to know which bend gets greasy after rain; I'm a mid-level operator on the lower end of the pay scale. My partner works night shifts at a care home, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. The car needed repairs last month, so our savings are under one month's expenses. I don't use AI tools, and I like to see a change work on another truck before it reaches mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the haul route will still need people who know the road. A bit less paperwork would be fine if it doesn't change our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is tight even with steady mine work. My partner's care-home night shifts can be cancelled, and we have little money ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving my assigned truck and checking tyres before the first load. I'd check last month's overtime shortfall against my shift record before the next mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the household money already, even if the AI story goes nowhere. The car repair left almost nothing between us and another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if another bill arrived tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the provider and ask to split the payment over two months. I would rather make that call than put it on a credit card and pay interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the paperwork tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the shift clerk use it first. If it makes the load record clearer, I can learn it, but I don't need a machine telling me how the road feels.

Check last month's **overtime shortfall** against my shift record before the next mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills and cancelled household shifts.
S0.quote: The car repair left almost nothing between us and another bill.
fieldNote: His **thin savings** and variable care-home shifts make household finances tense before automation adds any pressure.
He wants **proof** from a known colleague before accepting software, and his immediate concern is a missing overtime payment.

steps.text: Keep driving assigned haul truck and checking tyres each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schedulers should keep speaking to drivers when software changes load times. The mine needs to show a real roster before calling the change a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still drive the truck, but a leaner office could shorten my shifts. I don't know whether the new dispatch plan would leave room for weather delays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for two published rosters before changing our household budget. I'd record the rain delays on my route for the shift supervisor if targets rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because one lost overtime day matters to us. I don't want to learn a new screen on a promise alone, but I can show why the journey takes the time it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about a shorter shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd bring the rosters to the shift supervisor and ask what changed. If the answer is just that the computer says so, I'd speak with the workers' representative too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new dispatch screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the clerk has used it on real rainy days and can show me the steps. I don't use AI at home, and I won't pretend I understand a route calculation I haven't seen.

feel: **Anxious** that new rosters could remove overtime.
S1.quote: I won't pretend I understand a route calculation I haven't seen.
fieldNote: He sees **office scheduling** changing before truck driving, but expects lost overtime to hit the mortgage quickly.
He would gather **real rosters** and rain delays before taking a complaint beyond his shift supervisor.

steps.text: Compare two published rosters before changing the household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask when 2031 robot trucks would reach our route, not just when AGI arrives. Workers deserve written notice and help finding paid work before a fleet changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, office plans could change while I still drive loads. At 48 in 2031, I expect the mine to need fewer drivers and my shift could disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the depot manager about bus-driving openings before robot trucks arrive. I'd cut weekend restaurant meals this year to rebuild one month's emergency savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed by the fast picture. I have lain awake since the car bill thinking how quickly the house payment would fail if the truck wage went, and the 2031 date makes that feel close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bus depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot is one of the few large employers nearby, and I already know vehicle checks and long shifts. I don't know whether buses would also turn driverless, so I'd ask about their plans before paying for a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm checking other work and that they can keep their usual school routine for now. My partner and I would do the mortgage sums after our children are in bed.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely driver cuts and sleepless mortgage worries.
S2.quote: My partner and I would do the mortgage sums after our children are in bed.
fieldNote: The **2031 truck threat** turns an existing thin reserve into an expected loss of the household's main wage.
He considers a nearby **depot** but openly questions its durability if robot driving spreads beyond the mine.

steps.text: Ask nearby bus depot manager about paid driving openings and automation plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for 2034 truck dates while we have time to plan. Any new role should come with paid instruction, not just a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI may do dispatch and paperwork while I keep hauling. At 51 in 2034, the children will be older, but the mortgage will still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every second overtime payment into an emergency account until it holds a month. I'd ask the maintenance supervisor about a paid machinery course next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money now, though five years before the thinking change gives me time to check options. I'd need proof that a course leads to paid work before leaving the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to meet someone who finished the course and now works on the machines. A glossy sheet about future skills wouldn't be enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped the fitter identify a brake fault, and that part of the job interested me. Robots might also repair things in 2034, so I'd ask what work the course actually prepares people for.

say: I'd ask the company for **2034 truck dates** while we have time to plan.
Any new role should come with **paid instruction**, not just a new title.
think: At 48 in **2031**, AI may do dispatch and paperwork while I keep hauling.
At 51 in **2034**, the children will be older, but the mortgage will still need wages.
do: Put every second **overtime payment** into an emergency account until it holds a month.
Ask the **maintenance supervisor** about a paid machinery course next spring.
feel: **Anxious** about today’s budget, with time to verify options.
S3.quote: A glossy sheet about future skills wouldn't be enough for me.
fieldNote: A **2034 date** leaves him room to rebuild a small reserve and investigate training without giving up wages.
He remains **cautious** about maintenance as an escape, asking for evidence of paid work and robot exposure.

steps.text: Save every second overtime payment until emergency account covers one month
Ask maintenance supervisor next spring about paid machinery training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2039 is enough warning to tell drivers the truth about fleet plans. The mine should give every worker a dated letter, not a rumour at break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AGI could run dispatch while I still drive the truck. At 56 in 2039, I may still need a wage after our children have grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my haul shifts and check the mortgage balance with my partner twice a year. I'd ask the shift clerk for written fleet dates whenever the company updates them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the bank account is thin this year, not because 2039 is tomorrow. If the mine gives us real dates, I could make smaller choices without gambling the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know if we could afford that at 56. The children may be grown, but food, bills and whatever remains of the mortgage still have to be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider it only with a signed job offer and a clear plan for the family. There are few nearby mines, and moving for another truck job could leave us facing the same robot question.

say: I'd say **2039** is enough warning to tell drivers the truth about fleet plans.
The mine should give every worker a **dated letter**, not a rumour at break.
think: At 53 in **2036**, AGI could run dispatch while I still drive the truck.
At 56 in **2039**, I may still need a wage after our children have grown.
do: Keep my **haul shifts** and check the mortgage balance with my partner twice a year.
Ask the **shift clerk** for written fleet dates whenever the company updates them.
feel: **Anxious** about current finances despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: The children may be grown, but food, bills and whatever remains of the mortgage still have to be paid.
fieldNote: His **current balance** keeps him anxious, while a 2039 fleet change offers time to review plans gradually.
He rejects an assumed **retirement** at 56 and would require a signed offer before moving his family for mine work.

steps.text: Keep paid haul shifts and review mortgage balance with partner twice yearly
Ask shift clerk for written fleet dates after each company update

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot trucks could remove my wage in 2031 while both children are still in school and we've barely any savings. Written fleet dates, paid training that leads to real jobs, and help bridging a lost wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks whether a new job is actually there. I would want an employer's name and a pay rate before I tell my family to change everything.

headlineQuote: I would want an employer's name and a pay rate before I tell my family to change everything.
portrait: Felix is a **43-year-old** experienced haul truck driver with a vocational certificate and lower pay than many peers.
His partner's care-home shifts vary; two school-age children, a **mortgage** and thin savings make each overtime payment matter.
He avoids **AI tools** and wants to see a change work on familiar routes before trusting it.
A fast robot fleet leaves him **alarmed**; longer warnings let him verify training and rebuild a small reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robot trucks could remove his wage while the children still depend on it.
whatWouldHelp: **Written fleet dates**, paid training tied to jobs and income support would help him protect the mortgage.
